claims.text: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy lacks sufficient reactive aluminum to form a stable, protective oxide scale.
Laser surface alloying should be used to enrich approximately the top 50 μm of the surface with about 5 wt% aluminum.
Surface aluminum enrichment by laser alloying will promote formation of an Al2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure.
The resulting Al2O3 scale will be continuous and adherent.
At high temperature, the introduced surface aluminum reacts with oxygen to form Al2O3.
The Al2O3 layer will be thin and dense.
The Al2O3 layer will impede further oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
Impeded oxygen diffusion will reduce oxidation of the underlying alloy.
After 24 hours in flowing air at 900°C, the aluminum-enriched samples are expected to show approximately 30–50% less oxidation weight gain than untreated samples.
After the specified exposure, the aluminum-enriched samples are expected to have better oxide-scale integrity than untreated samples.
The comparison will use treated and untreated specimens exposed to flowing air at 900°C for 24 hours.
Changes in laser-processing parameters, substantially higher temperatures, or longer exposure durations may change the result.
The exact percentage improvement is an estimate requiring calibration.
The optimal aluminum concentration and depth profile for scale adhesion are unknown.
Laser-induced microstructural changes may affect mechanical properties.
The hypothesis is falsified if treated samples fail to achieve at least a 30% reduction in weight gain together with a more uniform and adherent Al2O3 scale relative to untreated controls.
